title: Your toddler doesn't need more toys this year. Research says fewer.
summary: Toddlers with 4 toys played longer and more creatively than with 16. What the research says before gift season, plus kind ways to ask grandparents for experiences.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo in a bright Houston living room on a November afternoon, landscape. A Black dad in his thirties with a close-cropped beard who uses a wheelchair leans forward, laughing, as his 2-year-old daughter with puffy pigtails sits on a low rug beside him and stacks big wooden blocks into a wobbly tower. Only a few toys are out: the blocks, a small wooden truck and a basket. Soft window light, a plant and a plain wall above them. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If you've ever stepped on a plastic dinosaur at 11 pm, looked at the overflowing toy bins and thought "how is this kid still bored?", you're in good company.
Gift season is coming, and with it the wish lists, the Black Friday deals on November 27 and the grandparents who love to shop. Before another box comes through the door, here's the good news.
The research suggests your toddler doesn't need more. Fewer toys may actually mean better play.
## The study that got parents talking

In [a 2018 study from the University of Toledo](https://www.bps.org.uk/research-digest/over-abundance-toys-may-stifle-toddler-creativity), researchers watched 36 toddlers, 18 to 30 months old, during two 15-minute play sessions. One time the room had 4 toys. The other time it had 16.
With 16 toys, the toddlers flitted. They had about 20 bursts of play, each lasting about a minute. With 4 toys, they had about 10, and each one lasted around two minutes.
They also played more creatively. With fewer toys, kids found about 60% more ways to use each one: stacking it, pretending with it, putting things inside it.
In other words, fewer choices gave kids room to go deep instead of wide.
## What the study can't tell us

To be fair, this was one small study in a lab, not your living room. The toys were new to the children, and new toys are extra distracting, so 16 unfamiliar toys may have pulled kids around more than 16 old favorites would.
Nobody has tested a "magic number" of toys for a home, and the study didn't test toy rotation either. But the finding fits with what pediatricians have said for years.
## What pediatricians say makes a good toy

In its [report on choosing toys](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/Best-Toys-Go-Back-To-The-Basics.aspx), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) puts it plainly: "The best toys need not be flashy or expensive or come with an app."
The best toys, the AAP says, are the ones that get parents and kids playing, pretending and interacting together. Electronic toys on their own don't give children that back-and-forth.

The AAP's [guide to play](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/family-life/power-of-play/Pages/The-Power-of-Play-How-Fun-and-Games-Help-Children-Thrive.aspx) suggests blocks, empty containers, wooden spoons, shape sorters and puzzles for ages 1 to 3. For 4- to 6-year-olds, it even says "some boredom allows for creativity." Consider that your permission to let them be a little bored.
And the line that might matter most: "It is parents and caregivers' presence and attention that enriches children, not fancy electronic gadgets."
## Try toy rotation (no decluttering marathon needed)

You don't have to give away half the playroom. Toy rotation means putting most toys away and bringing out a few at a time. It hasn't been studied directly, but it's a practical way to get the "fewer toys" effect without tears.
- **Sort into a few bins.** Mix types in each: something to build, something to pretend with, a vehicle, a puzzle or book.
- **Put out one bin at a time.** Store the rest in a closet, the garage or up high.
- **Swap every week or two,** or when interest fades. Old toys feel new again when they come back.
- **Keep true favorites out.** The lovey and the beloved fire truck don't rotate.
- **Follow your kid.** If they're deep into trains, leave the trains out longer.
## Asking grandparents for experiences, kindly
Grandparents give gifts because they love your kids. The trick is giving that love somewhere to go besides the toy bin.

There's some research on your side. Across [four studies](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/12/161215143300.htm) by Cindy Chan and Cassie Mogilner, experiences made people feel closer to the giver than physical gifts did, because experiences stir up more emotion. Those studies were with adults, but the idea is easy to borrow.
Some ways to say it that keep everyone happy:
- **Lead with thanks:** "She loves everything you give her. This year, could we do something together?"
- **Offer a short list:** a zoo or museum outing with Grandma, swim lessons, a class, or a "coupon" for a pancake breakfast date.
- **Suggest one toy plus one experience** if a gift to unwrap matters to them.
- **Point them to classics:** blocks, a puzzle or a few good books are the simple toys pediatricians love.
- **Make the memory visible:** a photo from the outing on the fridge reminds your child who gave it.
## Try this week
- Put half the toys in a closet for a week and watch what your child does with the rest.
- Set up 15 minutes of play with just 3 or 4 toys, and sit on the floor with them.
- Start a short "experiences" list to share with family before holiday shopping starts.
- Try a free outing that adds nothing to the toy bin, like storytime at Spring Branch Memorial Library on Corbindale Road.

If your playroom still looks like a toy store exploded, you haven't failed. You love your kid, and so does everyone who bought those toys. A few bins and a closet shelf can turn that pile into a lot more play.

title: Five days off school? You don't need zero screens. You need a plan.
summary: SBISD is out Nov 23–27. Why loose days turn into screen marathons, and a no-guilt plan that makes screens a tool, not the whole day.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo in a sunny Houston backyard on a cool late-November morning, landscape. A South Asian grandfather in his late sixties with silver hair, wire-rimmed glasses and a navy sweater kneels on a concrete patio, laughing as his 5-year-old granddaughter in a yellow hoodie draws a giant sun in sidewalk chalk and his 3-year-old grandson with a bowl haircut scribbles a long green line beside her. Chalk dust on their hands, soft morning light. The action sits low in the frame with live oak branches and pale blue sky above. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If you're already picturing Thanksgiving week as five straight days of cartoons, a sticky remote and a 4-year-old asking "one more?" for the ninth time, I see you.

Spring Branch ISD is out [Monday, November 23 through Friday, November 27](/guides/thanksgiving-break-spring-branch-2026/). That's a lot of hours to fill, plus cooking, travel and relatives who'd love your full attention.
Here's the good news: you don't need a screen-free break to have a good one. You need a loose plan, so screens are something you choose instead of the thing that fills every gap.
## Why breaks turn into screen marathons
It's not you. It's the calendar.

Researchers call it the [structured days hypothesis](https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC5530518). School days come with built-in structure, like a start time, recess and lunch at the same hour, and that structure quietly keeps kids' habits in check. On loose days, habits drift.

The researchers looked at 190 studies. In 155 of them, about 80%, elementary-age kids' habits (activity, screen time, eating and sleep) were less healthy on weekends than on weekdays. Most of this research is on school-age kids, and it shows patterns, not proof of cause. But anyone who has survived a rainy Saturday knows the feeling.
The takeaway isn't "screens are bad." It's that a little structure does a lot of the work for you.
## What the guidelines say (the short version)
We dug into the details in our [screen-time post](/blog/screen-time-young-kids-without-guilt/), so here's a quick refresher.

- **The World Health Organization's [guidelines](https://www.who.int/news/item/24-04-2019-to-grow-up-healthy-children-need-to-sit-less-and-play-more)** say screen time isn't recommended for babies under 1 or for 1-year-olds. For kids 2 to 4, it should be no more than 1 hour a day, and "less is better."

- **The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP)** [encourages families](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/news-releases/aap/2026/american-academy-of-pediatrics-calls-for-creating-a-child-friendly-digital-world/) to make a family media plan and to carve out screen-free spaces, like the car and dinnertime.

Here's a fun detail: the AAP's [guide to making a media plan](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/family-life/Media/Pages/How-to-Make-a-Family-Media-Use-Plan.aspx) says holiday breaks "are great times to review your plan." Consider this your official nudge.
Holidays are real life, though. A movie on Thanksgiving afternoon while the grown-ups cook won't undo anything. Guidelines describe everyday patterns, not one week in November.
## Use screens on purpose, not by default
The difference between a tool and a default is mostly timing.

- **Give screens a slot.** Pick one or two predictable times, like a show while you cook or a movie during the long Thursday afternoon. Kids handle limits better when they know when screens are coming.

- **Move first, watch later.** The CDC says [preschoolers should be active throughout the day](https://www.cdc.gov/physical-activity-basics/guidelines/children.html), and kids 6 and up need 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity a day. Get outside in the morning, and the afternoon show feels like a rest, not the whole day.
- **Choose a show, not a stream.** A movie or two episodes has a built-in ending. Autoplay doesn't.
- **Watch together when you can.** A family movie night is screen time and together time.
## Watch out for the calm-down tablet
Breaks are full of overtired, overstimulated moments, and the tablet is right there. Once in a while, that's survival. A pattern is worth noticing, though.

In [a 2022 study](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2022/12/221212140614.htm) that followed 422 parents of 3- to 5-year-olds for six months, kids who were often calmed with a device showed more trouble managing their emotions over time, especially boys. It's an observational study, so it can't prove the device caused it. But pediatrician Jenny Radesky, who led it, put it simply: a distraction "doesn't teach a skill."
Her alternatives are easy to try during a busy holiday week:
- **Get them moving.** Restless kids often need a jump, a swing or a big hug.
- **Name the feeling.** "You're so disappointed the show is over." It shows big feelings can be talked about and handled.
- **Use timers and clear rules,** so the end of screen time is never a surprise.
## A five-day break plan (no spreadsheet required)
Think of each day in three parts: an active morning, a quiet middle, and a screen slot you picked ahead of time.
- **Monday:** A long morning outside, like Terry Hershey Park or the Houston Arboretum. A show after lunch while everyone rests.
- **Tuesday:** A free indoor play spot or the library (check holiday hours). Then a blanket fort or a box of art supplies.
- **Wednesday:** Kids help cook: washing veggies, stirring, tearing bread for stuffing. A screen slot while you finish the hard parts.
- **Thursday:** Thanksgiving. A family movie while the turkey rests is a tradition, not a failure.
- **Friday:** Skip the stores. Try a slow walk or a playdate, then a pajama movie night.
Our [Thanksgiving break guide](/guides/thanksgiving-break-spring-branch-2026/) has more free and cheap ideas close to home.
## Try this week
- Take 10 minutes to pick the screen slots for the break, with your partner or on your own.
- Draw the plan on paper and show your kids, with little pictures for the ones who can't read yet.
- Pick one screen-free zone for the whole week, like the car or the Thanksgiving table.
- Fill a basket with crayons, play dough and puzzles for the moments between plans.

The goal isn't a perfect, screen-free week. It's a week where a show helps you get the pie in the oven, and your kids still remember the park, the fort and the rolls they helped butter. That's a great break.

title: Your toddler will skip the Thanksgiving nap. Here's how to survive it.
summary: A loud house, a late dinner and no crib in sight. How to save the nap, make a relative's home safe in 10 minutes and leave early without guilt.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo in a cozy guest bedroom at a relative's Houston home on Thanksgiving afternoon, landscape. A Middle Eastern dad in his thirties with a dark beard, thick wavy hair and a rust-colored sweater gently sways beside a portable play yard, his 10-month-old son in a soft sleep sack drowsy on his shoulder. A small white-noise machine sits on the nightstand. Through the half-open door, the blurred glow of a busy family gathering. Soft late-afternoon light through sheer curtains, a plain wall above, a calm and tender mood. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If you're already picturing Thursday afternoon (your 18-month-old wide awake at 2 p.m. in a guest room that smells like pie, cousins thundering past the door), you're in good company.

Thanksgiving with a baby or toddler isn't really about the turkey. It's about naps in strange rooms, a dinner that starts right at meltdown hour, and a house that was not set up for someone who puts everything in their mouth.
The good news: you don't need a perfect day. You need a decent plan, a 10-minute safety sweep and permission to leave early.
## Why one missed nap feels like a disaster (and why it isn't)

Little kids need a lot of sleep. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends [11 to 14 hours in 24 hours for 1- and 2-year-olds, naps included, and 10 to 13 hours for 3- to 5-year-olds](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4877308/).

So yes, you'll see it when the nap goes missing. In [a University of Colorado Boulder study](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2012/01/120103165012.htm), toddlers between 2½ and 3 who skipped just one nap showed 34% fewer happy reactions while doing puzzles they could solve, and 31% more negative ones on puzzles they couldn't.

That 5 p.m. meltdown is real, and it isn't bad parenting. But the study looked at how kids did that same afternoon. It doesn't show that one skipped holiday nap does lasting harm. A rough Thursday followed by a normal Friday is just a rough Thursday.
## Getting a nap in a loud, unfamiliar house
Your goal is to make a strange room feel like the same old nap.
- **Bring home's sleep cues.** The same sleep sack, white noise (a machine or a phone app), the same two books and the same song. A familiar routine does a lot of the work.
- **Claim the quietest room early,** as far as possible from the kitchen and the football game. Ask your host the week before so it isn't a scramble at the door.

- **For babies, pack the portable crib.** The AAP says babies should sleep on their backs on a firm, flat surface: [a crib, bassinet, portable crib or play yard that meets safety standards](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx), with no pillows, blankets or bumpers.

- **Skip the guest bed and the couch.** The AAP says the risk of sleep-related infant death is [up to 67 times higher when babies sleep with someone on a couch](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx). And if your baby dozes off in the car seat or stroller, move them to the play yard, on their back, as soon as you can.
- **Have a plan B for toddlers.** A stroller loop around the block or a quiet drive can rescue a nap that won't happen in the house.
- **Or nap at home.** If you're celebrating across town, the easiest nap is the one in their own crib. Arrive after it, or slip home for it and come back for pie.
## Timing dinner around your toddler
Holiday dinners love to land somewhere between 4 and 6 p.m., the exact hours when small people fall apart. Plan around it instead of hoping.
- **Feed them before the big meal.** A real snack or a mini-dinner an hour before means you're not counting on them eating at the table. (They may eat three rolls. That's fine.)
- **Let them leave the table when they're done.** Set up a quiet corner with a few books or a favorite toy so they can wander off without wandering into the kitchen.
- **Protect bedtime if you can.** If dinner runs late, do pajamas and teeth at the relative's house so the car ride home can turn into sleep.
## Make a relative's house safer in 10 minutes

Before you set your toddler down, do a quick lap. The stakes are real: Thanksgiving is the peak day for home cooking fires, with [more than three times the daily average](https://www.nfpa.org/education-and-research/home-fire-safety/thanksgiving), according to the National Fire Protection Association.

- **Kitchen:** the NFPA says [kids should stay three feet from the stove](https://www.nfpa.org/education-and-research/home-fire-safety/thanksgiving) and away from hot food and liquids. Keep knives, matches and lighters out of reach, and never leave a child alone in a room with a lit candle.

- **Bags and coats:** guests' purses, bags and jackets often hold medicine. HealthyChildren.org says to [keep them away from children's reach](https://healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/medication-safety/Pages/Medication-Safety-Tips.aspx), so start a pile in a closed room or up high. Look for pill organizers on counters and nightstands too.
- **Save Poison Help:** put [1-800-222-1222](https://healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/medication-safety/Pages/Medication-Safety-Tips.aspx) in your phone now, before you need it.

- **Stairs and cords:** the AAP's grandparent checklist suggests [gates at the top and bottom of stairs](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/A-Message-for-Grandparents-Keeping-Your-Grandchild-Safe-in-Your-Home.aspx) and moving dangling cords, like those from a coffeepot or toaster. Tuck away remote controls and anything with a small button battery.
- **The backyard:** if there's a pool, decide out loud which adult is watching the kids every time the back door opens. Busy holidays are when everyone assumes someone else has it.
## Leaving early is a plan, not a failure
Pick your exit time before you arrive and tell your partner, so nobody has to negotiate in the hallway with a screaming toddler on their hip. Pack the car during dessert.
If a relative pushes, keep it short and warm: "We're leaving while it's still fun." Nobody will remember that you left at 6:30. They'll remember that your kid was happy when they were there.
## Things to try this week
- Text your host: ask for a quiet room for naps and whether they have a gate.
- If your baby hasn't slept in the play yard lately, try a nap in it at home this weekend.
- Pack a sleep kit: sleep sack, white noise, two favorite books.
- Save 1-800-222-1222 in your phone (and your partner's).
- Agree on your leave-by time tonight.
Your toddler won't remember whether they napped on Thanksgiving. You might remember that you got to eat your pie while it was still warm.

title: The best gift for a toddler might not fit under the tree.
summary: Memberships, classes, books and together time: what experience gifts cost in Houston, which ages they suit, and the one research twist that makes them stick.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo on a wooden boardwalk by a pond at a wooded Houston nature center on a cool, sunny November morning, landscape. A Latino dad in his forties with a salt-and-pepper mustache crouches beside their curly-haired 4-year-old son in a red puffer vest, who points at a turtle on a log, while his husband, a white dad with a red beard, laughs with their 1-year-old daughter in a baby carrier. Tall trees and blue sky above, golden light. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If your phone already has three texts from grandparents asking "what does she want for Christmas?" and your honest answer is "less stuff," you're not alone.

After [our post on too many toys](/blog/too-many-toys-before-gift-season/), a lot of you asked the obvious next question: fine, then what *do* we give? Here's a list of gifts that won't end up in the toy bin, what they cost around Houston, and which ages they suit.
But first, one research twist that changes how to give them.
## The twist: little kids love things (and that's normal)

You may have read that experiences make people happier than stuff. For adults, that's mostly true. Across [four studies by Cindy Chan and Cassie Mogilner](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2016/12/161215143300.htm), experience gifts made people feel closer to the giver than material gifts did.

Little kids are different. In [four studies led by Lan Nguyen Chaplin](https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2020/11/201124123643.htm), children ages 3 to 12 got more happiness from material things than from experiences. Older teens flipped the other way.

Why? Lasting happiness from an experience depends on remembering it, and memory is still under construction in a preschooler. Chaplin says young kids are "ecstatic throughout the experience," but the glow fades if they can't recall the details.

The fix is easy: give the memory a handle. The researchers suggest taking photos or videos, because kids "are likely going to appreciate those experiences more if there is something to remind them of the event." A printed photo on the fridge does a lot of work.
So this isn't "experiences good, toys bad." It's one small, well-chosen thing to unwrap, plus a shared experience you help them remember.
## Memberships: the gift that keeps coming back
A membership turns one gift into a dozen outings, and it's a natural fit for a grandparent who wants to be part of them. Prices below are from each place's membership page this month:

- **Houston Arboretum & Nature Center:** the [Family Tree membership is $85](https://houstonarboretum.org/?p=39) for a family of four, and grandparents and grandchildren can count. It also gets you priority registration and lower prices on kids' nature programs and camps. Trails are free anyway, so this is a budget-friendly "supporter" gift with perks. Good for all ages, from stroller riders to bug hunters.

- **Children's Museum Houston:** the [Pathfinder level is $129](https://www.cmhouston.org/membership) for one adult and one child, which makes a sweet grandparent-and-grandkid gift. Family levels start at $199 for four people. Best for crawlers through early elementary kids.

- **Houston Zoo:** the [Family membership is $239](https://www.houstonzoo.org/membership/) for two named adults and up to three children ages 3 to 21. If you have a Lone Star card, there's an $89 Lone Star Family level. Animals are a hit from about age 1, and the zoo is a classic for 3- to 7-year-olds.
Tip: before buying, check the fine print on who has to be at the gate. Some memberships require a named adult at every visit.
## Classes and lessons

A class is a weekly experience with a built-in routine, and toddlers love routines. Think swim lessons (very useful in a city full of pools and bayous), a toddler music or movement class, or a caregiver-and-me nature program at the Arboretum.
- **Babies and young toddlers:** pick classes where a grown-up joins in. The point is time together, not skills.
- **Ages 3 to 6:** short drop-off or parent-nearby classes (swim, dance, art) start to make sense.
- **Gift it well:** wrap a swimsuit, ballet slippers or a paintbrush with the sign-up card, so there's something to open.
## Books (and a free one every month)

Books are the rare thing pediatricians actively want you to buy. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) [encourages shared reading from birth "continuing at least through kindergarten"](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/beyond-literacy-shared-reading-starting-in-infancy-offers-lifelong-benefits.aspx) and favors print books, noting that "digital books do not foster the equivalent parent-child interactions."
- **Babies:** board books with faces, textures or one picture per page.
- **Toddlers:** books with lift-the-flaps, rhymes and repetition they'll ask for 40 times.
- **Preschool and up:** picture books about their current obsession, whether that's trucks, dinosaurs or space.

And a free one: Harris County Public Library is part of [Dolly Parton's Imagination Library](https://hcpl.net/news/free-books-for-your-little-reader/). Children can start any time before age 3 and get a free book in the mail every month until they turn 5. You register in person at any HCPL branch, like Spring Branch Memorial Library on Corbindale Road.
## "Together time" coupons

The cheapest gift on this list may be the one your child remembers longest. The AAP says [the best toys are those that get parents and children "playing, pretending and interacting together"](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/news/Pages/Best-Toys-Go-Back-To-The-Basics.aspx), and a coupon book cuts out the toy entirely.
Ideas that work from about age 2:
- A pancake breakfast date with Grandpa.
- A "you pick the park" Saturday.
- A backyard campout or a flashlight walk around the block.
- Baking cookies together, mess included.
For little ones who can't read yet, draw a picture on each coupon. Then follow the research: take a photo during the date and tape it to the coupon afterward.
## Things to try this week
- Text the grandparents one experience idea and one small toy idea, before Black Friday on November 27.
- Pick one membership you'd actually use at least three times this year.
- Stop by your library branch and sign your baby or toddler up for free monthly books.
- Print a few photos from a recent outing and talk about them at dinner.
If the grandparents still show up with a giant singing truck, take a breath. Your kid will love it, and that's normal too. Gifts are just one way your child learns how many people love them.

title: One late night of holiday lights won't wreck your toddler's sleep. Promise.
summary: Tree lightings and movie nights start after dark, way past toddler bedtime. Here's what the sleep research says, plus how to do cold, crowds and fireworks with little ones.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo on a Houston park lawn at dusk in December, landscape. A Vietnamese American mom in her late twenties with a long black ponytail and her mother, a Mexican American grandmother with graying hair and a red scarf, sit on a plaid blanket. Between them a 3-year-old boy in fleece pajamas, knit hat and jacket points up in wonder; a baby dozes in a carrier on mom's chest. Warm string lights in bare branches and deep blue sky above. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If you're staring at a holiday events calendar and doing bedtime math ("the tree lights up at 6, so we'd get home at... oh no"), I see you. So many of the magical things happen after dark, and toddlers are not built for after dark.
Here's the reassuring part: one late night is a blip, not a setback. The research on kids' sleep is about what happens most nights, and a little planning makes the special nights a lot smoother.
## What the research actually says about one late night

Little kids need a lot of sleep. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine, with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) signing on, recommends [11 to 14 hours per 24 hours for 1- and 2-year-olds, and 10 to 13 hours for 3- to 5-year-olds](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4877308/), naps included. Notice the "per 24 hours": it's a daily total, so one short night is a small dent, not a crisis.

Missing sleep does show up fast, though, mostly in mood. In a [University of Colorado Boulder study](https://www.colorado.edu/today/node/2518), toddlers between 2½ and 3 who skipped a single nap had a 34 percent drop in positive reactions to a puzzle they could solve, and a 31 percent rise in negative reactions to one they couldn't. That's the science behind the meltdown in the parking lot.
So expect a cranky next morning, not lasting damage. And when your kid falls apart at 8:15 pm, that's tiredness talking, not a sign you made a mistake.
## Why the routine matters more than the clock

The big study here is reassuring for families who mostly have it together. In a [survey of 10,085 mothers in 14 countries](https://aasm.org/study-shows-that-children-sleep-better-when-they-have-a-nightly-bedtime-routine/), kids up to age 6 with a consistent bedtime routine fell asleep faster, woke less at night and slept longer. Kids with a routine every night slept more than an hour longer, on average, than kids who never had one.
The key word is consistency, and the benefit grew the more often the routine happened. One night out of seven doesn't erase the other six. You can even bring the routine with you:
- Put kids in pajamas before you leave, with a thin fleece jacket on top.
- Pack the bedtime book, the lovey and a small snack.
- Do the "wind down" part in the car: dim voice, soft music, the same goodnight phrase you use at home.
- When you get home, skip the bath and go straight to teeth, book, bed.
## Plan the night around your kid's clock
Houston helps a little here. In early December, the [sun sets around 5:21 pm](https://www.timeanddate.com/sun/usa/houston?month=12&year=2026), so lights look magical well before 7.
- **Go early, leave early.** Arrive at the start, see the main moment, and head out while everyone is still happy.
- **Protect the nap.** A good afternoon nap is the best insurance for a late night. For toddlers who've dropped naps, a quiet rest and an early dinner help.

- **Pick the right event.** Memorial Park's [Neighborhood Nights: Holiday Edition](/guides/holiday-events-santa-kids-spring-branch-memorial-2026/) on Fri Dec 4 starts *Frozen* at 6 pm, and there's no shame in leaving at intermission. CityCentre's Holiday in the Plaza on Sat Nov 28 is a daytime event, noon to 4 pm, if a late night isn't your family's thing this year.
- **Bring a carrier.** Neighborhood Nights doesn't allow strollers, and babies often doze off in a carrier anyway.
- **Have an exit plan.** Park near the edge, and decide ahead who takes the baby to the car if things go sideways.
## Cold, crowds and fireworks: the baby questions

Houston "cold" is mild, but a park lawn gets chilly fast after sunset. The AAP's rule of thumb is to [dress babies and young children in one more layer than an adult would wear](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-play/Pages/Cold-Weather-Safety.aspx) in the same conditions, plus a hat. Thin layers are easier to adjust than one bulky coat, and they're [the safe choice under car-seat straps](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/on-the-go/Pages/Winter-Car-Seat-Safety-Tips.aspx) on the drive home too.
If your baby falls asleep on the blanket, keep loose blankets away from their face. A wearable blanket or fleece suit is safer.

Fireworks are the one thing to think twice about. The AAP [advises keeping young children away from very noisy events like fireworks displays](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/news-releases/aap/2023/american-academy-of-pediatrics-sounds-the-alarm-on-excessive-noise-and-risks-to-childrens-hearing-in-updated-policy-statement/) and, if you go, using protective earmuffs, "including on young infants." It also warns that earplugs can be a choking hazard for little kids. The Mayor's Deck the Hall tree lighting downtown on Dec 5 ends with fireworks, so if you go, pack earmuffs and watch from farther back.

Crowds are more about comfort than danger. Keep toddlers in a carrier or on shoulders in a packed crowd, and agree on a meeting spot with older kids. And it's flu and RSV season, so a sick kid is a good reason to skip the night.
## Things to try this week
- Pick one evening event for the season and put it on the calendar now.
- Do a "pajamas under the jacket" test run on a short evening walk to see the neighborhood lights.
- Find earmuffs for any event with fireworks.
- Plan for a slow, cozy morning after the big night.
Years from now, your kid won't remember that bedtime was at 8:40 instead of 7:30. They might remember a sky full of lights, a cup of cocoa and your arms around them. That's worth one cranky morning.

title: Grandma wants to kiss the baby. In RSV season, you're allowed to say no.
summary: A newborn, a houseful of relatives and peak RSV and flu season. What pediatric guidance says about visitors, kisses and vaccines, plus kind scripts for saying no.

body: If you have a brand-new baby and a group chat already planning who's coming for the holidays, you might be feeling two things at once: so excited to show off this tiny person, and quietly panicking about every cough at the table.

Both feelings make sense. December is peak season for colds, flu and RSV, and newborns are the ones who get hit hardest. The good news is that a few clear rules, set ahead of time, do most of the protecting. You don't have to skip the holidays. You just get to be the boss of the baby.
## Why newborns need extra protection right now

A newborn's immune system "hasn't yet learned how to resist most infections," as the [American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) puts it](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/immunizations/Pages/How-to-Cocoon-a-Newborn-Only-an-E-Mail-Away.aspx). Babies are also too young for some vaccines: the first whooping cough shot doesn't come until 2 months, and flu shots start at 6 months.

RSV is the big one in winter. Before RSV immunizations, it was [the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the U.S.](https://www.cdc.gov/rsv/infants-young-children/index.html), and 2 to 3 out of every 100 babies under 3 months were hospitalized with it each year. To an adult, it usually feels like a cold.

Whooping cough (pertussis) is rarer but scary. [About 1 in 3 babies under 1 who catch it need hospital care](https://www.cdc.gov/pertussis/signs-symptoms/index.html), and many babies with it don't cough at all. And here's the part that matters for holiday planning: [many babies are infected by older siblings, parents or caregivers](https://www.cdc.gov/pertussis/about/index.html) who don't know they have it.
## Build a "cocoon" of vaccinated grown-ups

Pediatricians call it cocooning: the people closest to the baby get protected, so germs have a harder time reaching her. The [AAP recommends](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/immunizations/Pages/How-to-Cocoon-a-Newborn-Only-an-E-Mail-Away.aspx) that relatives, friends and caregivers be up to date on their flu and Tdap (whooping cough) shots, and finish Tdap at least 2 weeks before visiting. The [CDC says](https://www.cdc.gov/flu/highrisk/children.htm) the body takes about two weeks to build protection after a flu shot, too.
So if Grandma is flying in on December 20, now is the time to ask. Thanksgiving week is a perfect moment to bring it up.

For RSV, the protection is for the baby herself. The [CDC recommends one of two options](https://www.cdc.gov/rsv/vaccines/protect-infants.html): an RSV vaccine during weeks 32 to 36 of pregnancy, or an RSV antibody shot for babies under 8 months whose moms didn't get the vaccine. Most babies don't need both. If you're not sure your baby is covered, it's a quick question for your pediatrician.
## The house rules that actually help

Hand-washing isn't a cure-all, but it's real. Community hand-washing education [cuts colds and other respiratory illnesses by 16 to 21 percent](https://www.cdc.gov/clean-hands/data-research/facts-stats/index.html), and the CDC says to scrub for at least 20 seconds. The AAP is honest that hand-washing ["alone is not enough"](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/immunizations/Pages/How-to-Cocoon-a-Newborn-Only-an-E-Mail-Away.aspx), which is why it works best stacked with the other rules:
- **Wash before holding.** Every time, every person. Put a step stool at the sink so big cousins can do it too.
- **Sick people sit this one out.** A "little cold" or a scratchy throat means waving from across the room, or a video call.
- **No kisses on the face or hands.** Kiss the top of the head or the feet, or better yet, just admire.
- **Keep the holding circle small.** A few healthy, vaccinated people, not a pass-the-baby line around the living room.
- **Older siblings get a job.** The AAP suggests gently reminding little kids not to kiss the baby or get close when they're coughing. A 4-year-old can be the official "handwashing checker" instead.

The kissing rule has a serious reason behind it. Babies can catch the cold sore virus (herpes simplex) [from being kissed by someone with cold sores](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/001368.htm), and newborns whose infection spreads can get very sick. Anyone with a cold sore should stay away from the baby until it's healed.
## Kind scripts for awkward conversations
The hardest part usually isn't the science. It's telling your mother-in-law no. A few lines that keep it warm and firm:
- **Before the visit:** "We can't wait for you to meet her! Our pediatrician asked that everyone who holds her has a flu shot and Tdap. Could you get yours by the 5th?"
- **The kiss lean-in:** "Toes only until she's older! Doctor's orders."
- **The sniffly guest:** "I'm so sorry you're not feeling great. Let's video chat from the couch and do snuggles next time."
- **The skeptic:** "I know it feels like a lot. It's just for this season, and it helps me relax and enjoy the day."
Blaming the pediatrician is a time-honored move. Use it freely. You can also ask your partner to deliver the message to their own side of the family.
## Know the red flags

Even with every precaution, babies sometimes get sick. Call your pediatrician right away if a baby under 3 months has a [temperature of 100.4°F or higher](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/health-issues/conditions/fever/Pages/When-to-Call-the-Pediatrician.aspx). With RSV, watch for [trouble breathing, eating or drinking less, unusual fussiness or low energy, or pauses in breathing](https://www.cdc.gov/rsv/infants-young-children/index.html), and know that many babies with RSV don't have a fever. If your baby is struggling to breathe or turning blue, call 911.
## Things to try this week
- Text your holiday guests now about flu and Tdap shots, so there are two weeks to spare.
- Ask your pediatrician whether your baby has RSV protection.
- Set up a hand-washing spot near the front door or kitchen, with soap and a step stool.
- Pick your one-liner for the kiss lean-in and practice it out loud.
- Plan an escape room: a quiet bedroom where you and the baby can retreat when the house gets loud.
You're not being dramatic. You're being a parent of a newborn in December. The people who love your baby will understand, and next year she'll be the one handing out the kisses.

title: Two weeks of winter break doesn't need a schedule. It needs two anchors.
summary: SBISD is off Dec 21 to Jan 4. You don't need a color-coded plan to keep little ones sane, just steady sleep, a simple day shape and an easy way back.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo at a Houston neighborhood playground on a cool, sunny December morning, landscape. A white single mom in her early forties with a short blond bob, freckles and a green quilted jacket laughs at the bottom of a low slide, arms out to catch her 2-year-old son in a knit hat. Her 6-year-old daughter with a limb difference (left forearm ends below the elbow) and a brown braid climbs a rope net. Oak branches and pale blue sky above, golden light. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If you've already looked at the calendar and felt your eye twitch, same. SBISD's winter break runs from Monday, Dec 21 through Monday, Jan 4. That's two full weeks with no school drop-off, a toddler who still needs a nap, a kindergartner who is very, very awake, and a holiday or two dropped right in the middle.

Here's the relief: you don't need a color-coded plan for 15 days. The research points to a much smaller job. Keep sleep roughly steady, give each day a simple shape, and ease back in before school starts.
## Why bedtime is the one thing worth protecting

If you hold on to only one routine, make it bedtime. In [a UK study of 10,230 seven-year-olds](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24127471/), kids without regular bedtimes had more behavior problems, as rated by both moms and teachers. The best part: when kids switched from irregular to regular bedtimes, their behavior scores improved. That's not a forever verdict on your family. It's a lever you can pull anytime.

The routine before lights-out matters too. In [a study of 10,085 children from birth to age 5 across 13 countries](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4402657/), a consistent bedtime routine went with falling asleep faster, waking less at night and sleeping longer. More nights of the routine meant better sleep, but it didn't have to be perfect to help.
So on break, "roughly steady" is plenty:
- Keep bedtime within about 30 to 60 minutes of the school-night time on most nights.
- Keep the same few steps in the same order: bath or wash-up, pajamas, two books, a song, lights out. Even at Grandma's, the steps travel when the room doesn't.
- Protect the toddler nap at home on most days, and let it go on the busy days without guilt.

For a gut check, sleep experts recommend [11 to 14 hours in 24 hours for 1- and 2-year-olds, 10 to 13 hours for 3- to 5-year-olds (naps count), and 9 to 12 hours for 6- to 12-year-olds](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4877308/). If a late night happens, a slower morning or a longer nap usually evens it out.
## Give the day a shape: one outing, one at-home thing

Little kids don't need a packed schedule. They need to know what's coming. The CDC puts it simply: with predictable routines, ["kids feel safe and secure because they know what to expect."](https://www.cdc.gov/parenting-toddlers/structure-rules/index.html) ZERO TO THREE says routines help babies [build "trust and security"](https://www.zerotothree.org/resource/the-practical-magic-of-daily-routines/), which is exactly what goes wobbly when the days have no edges.
A loose shape that works for a lot of families:

- **Morning: one outing.** Get outside while everyone has energy. On a mild Houston day, try the forest-themed play area at Haden Park, the open space at Freed Park, or the paved trails at Terry Hershey Park for scooters and strollers.
- **Midday: lunch, then nap or quiet time.** Older kids who've outgrown naps can have an hour of books, puzzles or audiobooks in their room. Call it rest, not punishment.
- **Afternoon: one at-home thing.** A blanket fort, baking something easy, a sidewalk chalk mural, a long bath with cups. One thing, not a craft marathon.
- **Evening: the bedtime routine.** Same steps, same order.
Screens can fit into this shape too. Our [five-day break plan](/blog/screens-thanksgiving-school-break/) works just as well stretched over two weeks.

When plans change (a cold front, a sick cousin, a last-minute trip), the CDC suggests explaining it when you're both calm and saying whether the change is temporary. "No park today, it's raining. Tomorrow we'll go" is a whole conversation for a 3-year-old.
## When the big kid and the toddler are home all day
A 6-year-old and a 2-year-old together for 14 days is a lot of togetherness. Expect some friction. It isn't a sign anything is wrong.

The AAP suggests [fitting one-on-one time into your daily routines](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/family-life/family-dynamics/Pages/Sibling-Synergy.aspx), such as a chat at bedtime. During a break, nap time is gold for this:
- Use 20 minutes of the toddler's nap for the big kid's pick: a board game, a harder puzzle, a chapter book.
- Give the older child a toddler-free zone: a shelf, a box or a corner for their Legos and art.
- Hand them a real job if they want one ("Can you pick the books for your brother's bath?"), but don't make them the default babysitter.
## Getting back to normal by Jan 5

School starts again Tuesday, Jan 5. The AAP recommends helping kids [adjust to earlier bedtimes "a week or two before"](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/gradeschool/school/Pages/Back-to-School-Tips.aspx) the school year starts. After a short break you don't need that long, but a few days of runway beats one shocking alarm.
- Starting around New Year's Day, nudge bedtime and wake-up earlier by 15 minutes or so each day until you're back on the school schedule.
- Open the curtains and get everyone outside early on those last mornings, so the earlier wake-ups feel like part of the day, not a punishment.
- Talk about school a day or two ahead: who they'll see, what's for lunch, what they want to tell their teacher about the break.
- Expect a grumpy first week. That's the adjustment, not a failure.
## You're allowed to keep it small

Winter break doesn't have to be magical every day. Some days will be a park, a nap and frozen pizza, and that's a good day. Keep bedtime close, give the days a simple shape, and start the slide back a few days early. Everything else is extra, including the Pinterest crafts.
This week, try writing your family's "one outing, one at-home thing" list on a sticky note. Ten ideas is plenty. Then when Dec 21 arrives, you're not planning at 7 a.m. You're just choosing.

title: Your toddler won't sleep well at Grandma's the first night. Neither will you.
summary: A strange room, a play yard and a time change: why holiday trips scramble little kids' sleep, and the small, research-backed fixes that help them settle.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo in a cozy guest bedroom at a grandparents' home on a December evening, landscape. A Korean American dad in his thirties with black-rimmed glasses and a gray hoodie kneels beside a portable play yard, laughing softly as his 18-month-old daughter in a striped sleep sack stands holding the rail. His 4-year-old son in dinosaur pajamas sits cross-legged on the bed with a picture book. One small lamp gives a dim amber glow, a suitcase lies open on the floor, and a plain wall rises above them. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If you've ever stood in a dark guest room at 2 a.m., whisper-singing to a baby who is suddenly wide awake in a borrowed play yard, I'm right there with you. Holiday trips are full of good things: cousins, Grandma's cooking, someone else doing the dishes. Sleep usually isn't one of them.
Here's what helps: a rough first night is normal for little kids, and for grown-ups too. A few small, research-backed tricks can make night two (and the trip home) a lot easier.
This post is all about sleep. For car seats, flights and airport tips, see our [holiday travel guide](/blog/holiday-travel-with-little-kids/).
## Why the first night is the hardest

Sleep scientists have a name for it: the "first-night effect." In [a Brown University study of 35 adults](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4864126/) sleeping in an unfamiliar lab, one side of the brain stayed more alert during deep sleep, like a night watchman. It reacted more to strange sounds and woke people up more easily. By their next session in the lab, the effect was gone.

That study was in adults, so we can't say kids' brains do exactly the same thing. But pediatric sleep specialists see the pattern constantly. A Stanford Children's sleep doctor puts it plainly: ["kids don't sleep well in new environments"](https://healthier.stanfordchildrens.org/en/all-i-want-for-christmas-is-a-good-nights-sleep/), and you shouldn't "expect perfect sleep right away."
So if night one is choppy, it doesn't mean the whole trip is ruined. It means the room is new.
## Make the new room feel like home (and keep it safe)
Little kids sleep by routine and by smell, feel and sound. Bring those with you:

- Pack the familiar stuff: the same sleep sack, the lovey for kids old enough for one, and the same two bedtime books. The AAP even suggests [bringing your own crib sheet](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/on-the-go/Pages/Hotel-Dangers-that-Put-Baby-Safety-at-Risk.aspx) if your baby isn't used to new places.

- Do a trial run. If your baby will sleep in a play yard or your toddler in a travel bed, Stanford's sleep specialist suggests [trying it at home one to two nights](https://healthier.stanfordchildrens.org/en/all-i-want-for-christmas-is-a-good-nights-sleep/) before you leave.
- Keep the bedtime steps exactly the same, even if bedtime itself shifts. Bath, pajamas, books, song, lights out.

For babies, safe sleep comes along on the trip too. The AAP recommends putting babies [on their back, on a firm, flat surface, with only a fitted sheet](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/ages-stages/baby/sleep/Pages/a-parents-guide-to-safe-sleep.aspx), and avoiding bed-sharing, couches and armchairs. When you're exhausted at a relative's house, the AAP's advice is to [resist the big bed and use a portable crib or play yard](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/on-the-go/Pages/Hotel-Dangers-that-Put-Baby-Safety-at-Risk.aspx). A few quick checks when you arrive:
- Make sure a borrowed or hotel crib has no broken or missing parts and only its original mattress. Many hotels will lend one if you ask when you book.
- Set it up away from cords, lamps and TVs, or anything that could fall in.
- Leave Grandma's heirloom quilt and bumpers in the closet. A wearable blanket keeps baby warm instead.
## Dim the lights earlier than you think

Holiday evenings are bright: overhead lights, a glowing tree, a TV in every room. That matters more for little kids than we'd guess. In [a University of Colorado study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5835497/), an hour of bright light before bed cut preschoolers' melatonin, the hormone that makes us sleepy, by 87.6%. In most of the kids, it still hadn't bounced halfway back 50 minutes after the lights went off.
The study was small (10 kids, ages 3 to 5), but the lesson is easy to use:
- In the hour before bed, move your little one somewhere with lamps instead of overhead lights.
- Make the room dark. A spare blanket or a towel over a bright window works in a pinch.
- Keep it cool and quiet, not lit by a TV.

If you use white noise, mind the volume. In [a study of 14 infant sound machines](https://chop.edu/news/white-noise-not-right-noise), every one was louder than the 50-decibel limit for hospital nurseries at full volume, and some topped 85 decibels. Children's Hospital of Philadelphia suggests keeping the volume low and placing the machine (or phone) more than 200 centimeters, about 6 and a half feet, from the crib.
## One hour or two: handling the time change
Houston is on Central time, so Grandma on the East Coast is an hour ahead and the cousins in California are two hours behind. Here's what experts suggest:

- **Short trip (a few days)?** Stanford's sleep specialist says [staying on your home schedule](https://healthier.stanfordchildrens.org/en/all-i-want-for-christmas-is-a-good-nights-sleep/) will likely cause the least disruption. A 7:30 bedtime in Houston is just 8:30 in Atlanta.

- **Longer trip?** Shift naps and bedtime 30 to 60 minutes over a few days before you leave, earlier if you're heading east and later if you're heading west. The AAP's daylight saving advice works the same way: [nudge naps and bedtime a few minutes each day](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/healthy-living/sleep/Pages/daylight-saving-time-dont-lose-sleep-over-it.aspx) in the direction of the change.
- **Use the sun.** Light is one of the strongest cues for the body clock. After flying east, get outside early in the morning. After flying west, aim for afternoon sunshine.

- **Give it time.** Kids can take [three to four days](https://healthier.stanfordchildrens.org/en/all-i-want-for-christmas-is-a-good-nights-sleep/) to adjust to big time-zone shifts. One or two hours is usually quicker.
Thinking about melatonin or any sleep aid for the trip? Ask your pediatrician first, before you pack it.
## Pack it or pick it up there?
- **Pack:** the sleep sack, the lovey, the bedtime books, a familiar crib sheet, a nightlight, and your phone's white-noise app.
- **Pick up there:** diapers, wipes, snacks and bath stuff. They take up suitcase space and you can buy them almost anywhere.
- **Ask ahead:** whether the hotel or your relatives have a play yard you can use, so you can check it before bedtime instead of at bedtime.
## Lower the bar, then come home

Expect one rough night, maybe two. Then it usually gets better. A late bedtime at the family party won't undo months of good sleep. Once you're home, go right back to your usual routine and, as we said in our [winter break post](/blog/winter-break-routine-little-kids/), keep bedtime steady and the rest will follow.

This week, try a test night in the play yard or travel bed at home, and pack a "bedtime bag" with the sheet, sleep sack, books and lovey. Future you, standing in Grandma's guest room at bedtime, will be glad you did.

title: The riskiest thing under the tree this year might be the size of a coin.
summary: Button batteries, tiny magnets and water beads hide in holiday gifts and decor. What pediatricians want you to check before the wrapping paper flies.
imagePrompt: A warm, realistic, candid photo in a cozy Houston living room on a December afternoon, landscape. Two moms sit on a rug by a small decorated tree: a Filipina American mom in her thirties with a pixie cut and hearing aids reads a toy box, smiling, while her wife, a curvy white mom with curly auburn hair and a cream sweater, laughs as their 20-month-old son tugs tissue paper from a gift bag. Their 5-year-old daughter hands over a present. Soft window light, plain wall above. No text, signs, logos or brand names.
body: If your toddler's favorite part of a present is the bow, the box and anything small enough to fit in their mouth, you're in good company. Little kids explore with their mouths. That's normal, healthy and also exactly why December keeps ER doctors busy.

I'm not here to make you scared of gifts. Most toys are fine. But three small things show up again and again in pediatric safety warnings this time of year: button batteries, tiny magnets and water beads. A few quick checks before (and right after) the unwrapping go a long way.
Forward this one to the grandparents. They're doing a lot of the shopping.
## Button batteries: small, shiny and hiding everywhere

Button and coin batteries are the flat, round ones about the size of a coin. If a child swallows one, it can set off a chemical reaction that [damages or burns through the esophagus (the food pipe) within 2 hours](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/what-parents-need-to-know-about-button-and-lithium-coin-batteries.aspx), according to the AAP. Even a "dead" battery [still carries enough charge to burn tissue](https://connecticutchildrens.org/growing-healthy/dangers-water-beads-button-batteries-and-magnets), an emergency physician at Connecticut Children's warns.

This isn't rare. A study in *Pediatrics* found [an estimated 70,322 battery-related ER visits among U.S. children from 2010 to 2019](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/news-releases/pediatrics2/2022/battery-related-pediatric-emergency-department-visits-more-than-double), about one every 1.25 hours, with most among kids 5 and younger. About 90% of those visits were for swallowed batteries.

The tricky part is where they hide. The AAP's [holiday walkthrough](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/small-battery-safety-at-home-a-winter-holiday-walkthrough.aspx) lists:
- Light-up decorations: flameless candles, ornaments, wreaths and garland
- Musical greeting cards and children's books that play sounds
- Remote controls, key fobs, light-up shoes and new electronic toys
- Kitchen scales, meat thermometers and digital bathroom scales
- Hearing aid batteries in a visiting relative's purse or nightstand

The fix is simple: make sure your child can't open the battery compartment, and if it isn't closed with a screw, [tape it shut](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/small-battery-safety-at-home-a-winter-holiday-walkthrough.aspx). Keep spare and used batteries up high and out of sight, and recycle old ones soon.
## Magnets: one is a worry, two is an emergency

A single small magnet usually passes. The danger is [swallowing two or more](https://www.seattlechildrens.org/health-safety/injury-prevention/dangers-button-batteries-magnets/), which can stick together through the walls of the intestines and cause serious injury or death. Seattle Children's says surgery may be needed to remove them.

The worst offenders are the powerful little magnetic balls and cubes sold as desk toys or fidgets for older kids and adults. Seattle Children's says [young children should never play with magnets](https://www.seattlechildrens.org/health-safety/injury-prevention/dangers-button-batteries-magnets/). If a big sibling, teen cousin or uncle unwraps a set, it needs a home well out of reach.
Check toddler toys, too. Magnetic tiles and building sets made for little kids are designed to hold their magnets in, but a cracked piece can let one loose. If you find a broken one, toss it.
## Water beads: the squishy craft that grows inside

Water beads are tiny, colorful gel balls that look like candy. The CPSC says they [can grow up to 100 times their size in water](https://www.cpsc.gov/node/66135). Swallowed, they can keep swelling and [block the bowel, ears, nose or airway](https://connecticutchildrens.org/growing-healthy/dangers-water-beads-button-batteries-and-magnets).

The CPSC lists [swallowing water beads among the most common causes of toy-related deaths](https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2025/Happy-Holidays-Start-with-Safety-CPSC-Urges-Families-to-Cook-Decorate-and-Select-Toys-with-Care-This-Season). A new federal rule now limits how big toy water beads can grow and requires warning labels, but [it covers toys made after March 12, 2026](https://www.cpsc.gov/node/66135), so older stock can still be out there. Beads sold for vases and plants aren't covered.
My honest take: with babies, toddlers or preschoolers in the house, skip them. Sensory bins work just as well with dry pasta, big pom-poms or rice under supervision.
## The 30-second toy check
You don't need a lab. Before wrapping, or as gifts come out of the paper:

- **Read the age label and follow it.** The CPSC says to [keep toys with small parts away from kids under 3](https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2025/Happy-Holidays-Start-with-Safety-CPSC-Urges-Families-to-Cook-Decorate-and-Select-Toys-with-Care-This-Season) and deflated balloons away from kids under 8.

- **Try the toilet paper roll test.** If a toy or a piece of it [fits inside an empty roll, it's too small for a baby or toddler](https://ukhealthcare.uky.edu/blog/post/safe-holiday-season-toy-safety-tips). It's a handy guide, not a guarantee.
- **Check for batteries and magnets.** Look for a screwed-shut battery door and no loose magnets.

- **Clear the packaging fast.** The CPSC advises [throwing away plastic wrap and packaging right after gifts are opened](https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2025/Happy-Holidays-Start-with-Safety-CPSC-Urges-Families-to-Cook-Decorate-and-Select-Toys-with-Care-This-Season). Those twist ties and tiny plastic bits end up in mouths, too.
- **Sort big kids' gifts.** Older siblings' tiny-part sets get their own table or room, with a "bins up high" rule.
## If you think your child swallowed something
Don't wait for symptoms. A child who swallowed a battery can seem completely fine at first.

- **Button battery:** the AAP says to [go to the emergency room or call 911](https://www.healthychildren.org/English/safety-prevention/at-home/Pages/what-parents-need-to-know-about-button-and-lithium-coin-batteries.aspx) right away. Don't make your child throw up. The AAP says kids over 12 months who can swallow can get 2 teaspoons of honey on the way, but never delay care to find it. The National Battery Ingestion Hotline is 800-498-8666.
- **Magnets or water beads:** if you think your child swallowed more than one magnet or any water beads, get emergency care.
- **Call 911** for choking, trouble breathing, drooling, or vomiting.
## You've got this
The point isn't a perfectly baby-proofed December. It's a few minutes of looking with fresh eyes: at the singing card, the flameless candles, the cousin's magnet set.
This week, try this:
- Walk your house with the AAP list above and tape any loose battery doors.
- Save the battery hotline, 800-498-8666, in your phone and your partner's.
- Send this post to the grandparents before they wrap anything.
Then enjoy the part your toddler actually loves: the box.
